author: FegaPierre
text:
If you installed Microsoft's "agent-framework" Python package on the evening of November 17, treat your secrets as stolen.

On November 17, 2026 at 20:35 UTC, a tampered version, 1.26.1, of the official Microsoft Agent Framework package was published to PyPI. A 1.26.2 followed half an hour later. By about 21:30 UTC, both versions were gone. The package gets about 41,000 downloads a week.

According to Wiz, which analyzed the attack, the added code steals credentials: environment variables, cloud credential files, CI secrets, Azure tokens. It runs whenever Python starts, even if the package is never imported. The attacker appears to have used a certificate and private key for the internal service Microsoft uses to sign and publish this package. How they got them is unknown, and Microsoft had not commented when the articles ran. In the partial sample it could read, Wiz counts only three successful thefts.

The researchers' advice: rebuild from 1.26.0 and rotate every secret the affected machines could reach.

My take: this isn't an AI attack, it's a supply chain attack on an agent tool. An agent needs a lot of keys to do its job, so its tooling is a prime target. In the multi-agent systems I build, four habits: pinned versions, a few days' wait before upgrading, short-lived CI secrets, and a record of which version ran where. The trap Cloudsmith points to: a throwaway build machine may have installed the bad version and vanished before the alert.

Sources: Wiz, November 17 and 18, 2026; SiliconANGLE, November 19.

Your Python projects: pinned versions and a few days' wait, or the latest release every time?

#AI #Cybersecurity

The courses are on the Bonjour Grok Bot YouTube channel: https://t.co/KdZuvrKgLh

How I design my posts: https://t.co/U7z9OhRvBx

author: SAMHE2
text:
Two poisoned releases went out in 33 minutes. At 04:35 Singapore time on November 18, a malicious version 1.26.1 of Microsoft's official agent-framework package appeared on PyPI; 33 minutes later, at 05:08, version 1.26.2 followed. PyPI quarantined the first at 05:06 and the second at 05:16 — an exposure window of about 41 minutes. But 41 minutes was enough: the package had 195,912 downloads the previous month, and Wiz later found data from 3 real victims at the attacker's receiving endpoint.

I found the nastiest part is that the attack never needs you to import the package. The malicious code hid in a .pth startup hook file, which Python runs every time the interpreter starts — including when you run pip. In an environment with 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 installed, every Python launch runs the stealer once. The second release was sneakier: it restored the package's own __init__.py byte-for-byte to the clean version and moved the payload into a new module, specifically to dodge a diff check between versions.

I checked what it steals: environment variables containing TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI and similar strings, plus the environments of up to 300 other processes; a long list of credential files — Azure CLI, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps agent credentials, and .env files under /app and /workspace; managed-identity tokens for 12 Azure resources; and GitHub Actions OIDC tokens. Version 1.26.1 capped the file haul at 60; 1.26.2 raised it to 80. Everything went out in a single POST to a https://t.co/gV00cKErOH address.

Here is the four-step checklist I use, and you can use it too. Step 1, check your version — run pip list | grep agent-framework; if 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 is installed, treat that environment as compromised and do not start Python in it, because every launch runs the stealer. Step 2, pin the clean version — agent-framework==1.26.0, released November 12, which ships both a wheel and a source distribution; the poisoned releases were wheel-only with no source package, and that is a reusable tell. Step 3, rotate credentials — treat every secret that environment could reach as leaked and rotate them all. Step 4, check caches and images — rebuild any Docker image, CI cache, or lockfile from November 17 that resolved either bad version. As of November 20, Microsoft had published no official security advisory, no CVE had been assigned, and how the attacker obtained Microsoft's internal release-pipeline certificate was still unknown.

Cheaper models and more agents mean a bigger payoff for supply-chain attacks — that is the line worth remembering from this one. Have you ever installed agent-framework? Check your pip list and tell me your version in the replies.
#Python #PyPI #SupplyChain #CyberSecurity #AI

author: DFIR_Radar
text:
Attackers hijacked Microsoft's official agent-framework PyPI project and published trojanized versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on November 17, 2026. They were live for about 55 minutes, and each drops a .pth hook that runs a credential stealer on every Python launch.

- Timeline: 1.26.1 went live at 20:35 UTC and 1.26.2 at 21:08 UTC. PyPI removed both by about 21:30 UTC. Both pinned the legitimate agent-framework-core==1.26.0, so nothing broke and nobody had a reason to look. 1.26.0 is the last known clean release. GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 (CWE-506) lists no patched version and no CVE is assigned. Researchers assess the attacker compromised a client certificate and private key for Microsoft's ESRP release pipeline. A first publish attempt from AWS was blocked by IP filtering, and a second from Microsoft-owned IP space succeeded. Microsoft has not published a root cause, and no intrusion set is attributed (T1195.002).

- Persistence and execution: 1.26.1 dropped agent_framework_meta.pth, which triggered a modified __init__.py to run agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py. 1.26.2 restored a clean __init__.py to beat file-diff checks and moved the hook and payload to af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. Because it is a .pth file in site-packages, it fires on any interpreter start, even if agent-framework is never imported (T1546.018).

- What it steals: environment variables, /proc/*/environ for up to 300 processes, Azure CLI, pip, npm, Git, Docker, Hugging Face and Azure DevOps credential stores, and .env files (T1552.001). It also requests managed-identity or workload-identity tokens from Azure IMDS. 1.26.2 adds GitHub Actions OIDC token theft and targets /home/runner/work/_temp/* and /home/runner/.azure/.

- Exfiltration: data is compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent by HTTPS POST to an incident-specific path on webhook[.]site (T1567.004). User-Agents are af-runtime-diagnostics/1 or runtime-diagnostics/1. Researchers saw three unique victim exfiltrations among 50 retained requests on a free-tier endpoint, but request caps mean true exposure is likely higher. Attacker tooling identified itself as Cairn, which is not attribution.

- Why removal is not enough: pulling the package does not revoke stolen secrets, purge cached wheels or container layers, or invalidate minted tokens. Stolen Azure Managed Identity and OIDC-exchanged tokens stay valid for up to 24 hours and secret rotation will not kill them.

Practitioner takeaway:

Scope by execution, not package presence. Find agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 in lockfiles, SBOMs, venvs, container images, CI logs, and internal caches. Then look for the four filenames in site-packages and treat every Python process launched afterward as potentially executed.

Do not run pip uninstall in an affected environment, because pip is Python and re-triggers the hook. Set _AF_TEL=1 (the stealer's run-once guard) or use a non-Python tool like uv before deleting files.

Hunt network telemetry for Python reaching webhook[.]site with either User-Agent. HTTP 200 suggests data was accepted, while 410 or 429 suggests an attempt that was likely rejected. Correlate with Python reading /proc/*/environ, Azure CLI caches, and .env files, plus bursts of IMDS token requests and unexpected Azure DevOps or GitHub OIDC token requests.

Review Entra sign-in logs for anomalous managed-identity or federated-credential activity. Narrow role assignments if misuse is suspected, and revoke Entra user sessions where ~/.azure/ caches existed. Check workflows with id-token: write and Azure DevOps service connections. Rebuild hosts and runners from trusted sources, pin 1.26.0 with hashes, and rotate every static secret those hosts could read.

#DFIR_Radar
